items.title: 21.1.2 Defence Provided by Digestive and Respiratory Tracts

source_refs.note: Topic 21.1.2 (PDF 171-172); Figure 21.3 is replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: Food carries many bacteria. Most are killed by saliva in the mouth, which also contains lysozyme, and by the strong acid in the stomach and the protein-digesting enzymes of the intestine.

The air we breathe also carries many microbes. Ciliated epithelial cells in the nasal cavity trap many bacteria before they enter the airway. The cells lining the smaller bronchi and bronchioles secrete sticky mucus that traps microbes before they reach the warm, moist lungs, and cilia on these cells keep sweeping the mucus upward, where it can be swallowed.

blocks.alt: The lining of the trachea: a row of tall cells, most with cilia on top and two goblet cells holding mucus. Above them a yellow layer of sticky mucus holds green microbes, and an arrow shows the cilia sweeping the mucus towards the throat.
blocks.caption: Cilia and mucus in the airway lining (original diagram after Figure 21.3).
blocks.long_description: Ciliated epithelial cells in the nasal cavity trap many bacteria before they enter the airways. Cells lining the smaller bronchi and bronchioles secrete sticky mucus that traps microbes before they reach the warm, moist lungs, and the cilia keep sweeping the mucus upward to the throat, where it is swallowed and the microbes are destroyed by stomach acid.

blocks.prompt: Why does swallowing mucus from the airways help defence?
blocks.explanation: The trapped microbes are carried to the stomach, where strong acid kills them.

items: Digestive tract: lysozyme in saliva, stomach acid, intestinal enzymes.
Airways: cilia trap microbes; mucus is swept up and swallowed.
